articles.title: Diana Shnaider praises ‘very dangerous’ Alex Eala after knocking her out of the Ningbo Open
articles.summary: Alexandra Eala’s Ningbo Open campaign has come to an end. The Filipina star was unable to overcome the challenge presented by Diana Shnaider on Thursday,...
articles.body:
Alexandra Eala's Ningbo Open campaign has come to an end.

The Filipina star was unable to overcome the challenge presented by Diana Shnaider on Thursday, falling to a 5-7, 4-6 defeat in the Chinese province.

Shnaider, who is still fighting for a WTA Finals alternate spot, will play American youngster Iva Jovic in the Ningbo Open quarter-finals.

The Russian star, who reached the Roland Garros semi-finals in June , made sure to credit her opponent's quality during the post-match formalities on Thursday.

Diana Shnaider praises Alex Eala after triumphing in Ningbo

"I mean, definitely much better than my previous one," Shnaider said with a chuckle, comparing her performance against Eala to her one against Yulia Putintseva in the first round.

"Obviously very happy the way I played today, the way I compete, because definitely Alex is very dangerous and a tough opponent.

"Another lefty, another big hitter. She never goes back down, she steps in, she rips the ball. So I knew it was going to be tough. Very proud and happy the way I performed today."

Shnaider was then asked to discuss the tactical adjustments she makes when playing a left-handed player. Shnaider, like Eala , is also left-handed.

"It's never easy to play another lefty – it's not very often," the 22-year-old Russian said. "And not very often we have to practice with each other.

"I would say you kind of expect another spin, especially the slice serve into the body. Yeah, definitely a little more variation, different type of ball strike.

"But again, you talk through it, I feel like you gotta just get used to the ball. I guess first few games you just kinda get used to the spin – where is her strike zone, what is her weakness.

Ningbo Open second round: lost to Diana Shnaider 5-7, 4-6

Ningbo Open first round: defeated Diane Parry 6-3, 6-1

Wuhan Open first round: lost to Shi Han 6-4, 3-6, 3-6

Singapore Open: lost to Tatiana Igorevna Prosorova 6-4, 5-7, 3-6

US Open: lost to Iva Jovic 5-7, 6-3, 5-7

"And you just gotta give yourself a little bit more time to adjust and then it becomes a little bit easier when the game goes on."

As mentioned previously, Shnaider will play Iva Jovic in the Ningbo Open quarter-finals.

Shnaider has played Jovic once before, losing to the American at the 2026 Dubai Tennis Championships, 4-6, 6-1, 0-6.

After losing in Ningbo, Eala will shift her attention to the Toray Pan Pacific Open , held in Tokyo, Japan.

Eala is set to compete in the WTA 500 event alongside a host of high-profile names, including world number one Elena Rybakina and recent Wuhan Open champion Maja Chwalinska .

Belinda Bencic, the defending champion, is also set to compete in this year's event, which will run from October 26 to November 1.

A total prize pot of $1,206,446 is on offer to singles and doubles players at the 2026 tournament.

articles.title: La ATP censura más de 234.000 comentarios ofensivos contra jugadores y aficionados
articles.standfirst: El proyecto ATP Safe Sport, lanzado en 2024, analizó más de 3,7 millones de comentarios en las redes sociales del máximo organismo del tenis
articles.summary: El proyecto ATP Safe Sport, lanzado en 2024, analizó más de 3,7 millones de comentarios en las redes sociales del máximo organismo del tenis
articles.body: La ATP, el máximo organismo del tenis profesional, lanzó en 2024 ATP Safe Sport. Un proyecto, junto con Tennis Data Innovations (TDI), dedicado a proteger el bienestar de los jugadores y aficionados. Este jueves, ha salido a la luz un comunicado oficial en el que se informa de la censura de más de 234.000 mensajes ofensivos, que se han detectado en las redes sociales del organismo y de los propios tenistas. El programa oficial, que mezcla moderación de mensajes, evaluación de amenazas y colabora con las autoridades policiales, todo de la mano de la inteligencia artificial, ha analizado alrededor de 3,7 millones de comentarios en los canales de la ATP y jugadores: "Se identificaron más de 284.000 comentarios ofensivos, pudiendo eliminarse el 82% de ellos en tiempo real antes de que llegaran a jugadores y aficionados", según cuenta el comunicado oficial. Hace dos semanas, la estadounidense Coco Gauff denunció insultos racistas tras su encuentro ante Sun Xinran en el WTA 1000 de Pekín. Andrew Azzopardi, director de seguridad de la ATP, ha alzado la voz: "El bienestar de los jugadores es un pilar fundamental de las labores de seguridad de la ATP. Impedir que llegaran más de 234.000 comentarios ofensivos es el reflejo del impacto tangible que el programa tiene cada día. No hay lugar para la violencia digital en el tenis. Seguiremos invirtiendo en tecnología, experiencia y colaboraciones para proteger a los jugadores, y seguiremos trabajando con las autoridades para exigir responsabilidades a quienes cometan estos actos”. La Federación Internacional de Tenis (ITF), la WTA y las organizaciones encargadas de Roland Garros, Wimbledon y US Open (FFT, All England Club y USTA, respectivamente) ya han incluido en sus programas servicios de inteligencia artificial y control de datos públicos con el fin de prevenir comentarios abusivos. En el caso del Grand Slam francés, ha habilitado un software con IA a los jugadores para bloquear el acoso digital.

articles.title: Andy Murray’s wife Kim Sears and their four children: How family life has evolved since the former tennis champion retired from professional tennis and embraced fatherhood
articles.summary: Discover how former tennis champion Andy Murray has embraced family life, fatherhood, and business after retiring from professional tennis. Learn how Murray balances parenting with his ongoing connection to the sport and his role in managing Cromlix, the family hotel.
articles.body: Andy Murray’s life changed dramatically when he retired from pro tennis at the 2024 Paris Olympics. The former British champion has adapted to a different lifestyle with wife Kim Sears and their four children following years of international travel, rigorous training schedules and big tournaments. Recent interviews have also shown how much he is enjoying the extra time at home after spending a good portion of his playing career away from his family.The couple have daughters, Sophia, Edie and Lola, and son, Teddy. Murray’s connection to tennis is still strong through his experience and continuing interest in the sport, but retirement has created more time for normal parenting and family activities. They also own Cromlix, the Scottish country-house hotel, which means the couple have a business interest in common beyond the tennis circuit.How Andy Murray enjoys family life after tennis retirementFor Murray, retirement has been about showing up for the moments that were difficult to be present for consistently in his playing career. Professional tennis demanded long periods of travel between tournaments, training facilities and recovery sessions. Sometimes his family joined him on the tour, but inevitably the schedule curtailed the amount of unstructured time he could spend with his children.Murray said in a July 2026 interview that he liked retirement and having more time with his children. He admitted he’d been away a lot of his career and had missed his family often. The change has meant he can enjoy many of the routines that many parents take for granted, rather than family time dictated by an international competition calendar.The adjustment also demonstrates how the priorities of the couple have changed over time. Murray and Sears had children while he was still playing at the top level. Their eldest daughter Sophia was born in 2016, then Edie in 2017, Teddy in 2019 and their youngest daughter Lola in 2021. The children grew up during different stages of Murray's career, including times of injury, recovery and his eventual retirement.Family life now provides a different pace from the pressure of professional competition. Murray will be able to spend more time with his children and nurture their interests as they grow up. He has previously spoken of the importance of being a good father, making it clear that fatherhood is a priority separate from his sporting achievements.The change doesn't mean that tennis has disappeared from his life. Instead, it has changed its role in his daily routine. Murray’s schedule was shaped by years of matches and training, and he has had more freedom to pursue other interests, spend time with his family and consider opportunities related to the sport without the same pressure of competing on tour.Kim Sears’ background, artistic career and marriage to Andy MurrayKim Sears has been in Murray’s life since they were teenagers. The pair first met at the US Open in 2005 when Sears was still at school, and Murray was on the way up in the professional game. Their relationship developed with his career, and the rigors of international competition were brought into their home. They tied the knot on 11 April 2015 at Scotland’s Dunblane Cathedral.Sears has tennis in his blood, too. Her father, Nigel Sears, is a former professional player and well-respected coach. Raised in the sport, she understands the demands it puts on you, though she has developed her own interests outside her husband’s career.Art is one of those hobbies. Sears is known for her portraiture and animal paintings, and she has maintained a fairly private public profile despite Murray’s international fame. Her creative work has also informed her involvement with Cromlix, shaping the interiors, artwork and overall atmosphere of the hotel.The couple bought a Victorian country house, Cromlix, near Dunblane in 2013. The property has a personal significance for Murray's family and a linkage to the local community. The couple have since turned the estate into a hospitality business, with Sears playing a key role in its creative direction since taking ownership. The hotel has therefore become a common project that unites family ties, design and business.From this, their partnership has grown beyond the public persona of a tennis champion and his wife. Sears has been there for Murray through the highs and lows of his playing career, but she has also continued to develop her own artistic interests and played an active role in the couple's business. Parenting is still a big part of life’s daily routine, but retirement has brought them a new avenue to share their time and responsibilities.How Andy Murray balances fatherhood and life beyond tennisMurray’s own approach to fatherhood has been influenced by his experience of raising children through a demanding professional career. The couple have largely kept their children away from too much public exposure, allowing them to grow up away from the constant attention that comes with their father’s sporting achievements.The family has still given glimpses of life together now and then. Previously, the comedian has talked about the ups and downs of being a parent, from taking part in activities his daughters pick to the realities of keeping children amused. He also discussed the strange opportunity of spending long periods of time at home during the COVID-19 lockdown, while admitting that lending a hand with children’s education could be a challenge.The obligations of professional life against domestic life are different now that he is no longer playing. Murray no longer has to structure his whole year around tournaments, travel and physiotherapy. This flexibility allows him to be more involved in his kids’ routines and to enjoy family experiences without needing to be away from home for extended periods.The family’s link to Cromlix means their private and professional lives are also intertwined. The hotel is more than just a business; it is part of the couple’s family history and relationship with Scotland. Their children visit the property, and the estate offers the family a connection between their current life and Murray’s roots in Dunblane. In an interview in June 2026, the couple talked about their family visits to Cromlix and what the property means to them personally.Murray’s life outside tennis is still being built, and his continuing relationship to the sport means retirement isn’t a total departure from the world that defined much of his adult life. But the emphasis has shifted. His family, his interests away from the court and the couple’s work at Cromlix now have more space to sit alongside his tennis legacy.For Murray and Sears, the next few years will mean new stages of parenthood as their children grow and develop their own interests. In their case, retirement isn’t so much about filling the void of major tennis triumphs as about clearing the decks for another kind of achievement: showing up for family life after years molded by the pro tour.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Felix Balshaw: How the son of an English rugby legend represents France
articles.summary: Felix Balshaw is the son of an English Rugby World Cup winner - but is representing France as he climbs the world tennis rankings.
articles.body:
Accents quickly reveal a lot about a person.

So speaking to Leeds-born Felix Balshaw - the 20-year-old son of England Rugby World Cup winner Iain - it soon becomes clear why he is representing France on his climb up the professional tennis ladder.

There is no mistaking a strong Gallic twang as Balshaw, who celebrated the first ATP Tour victory of his career this week, discusses his journey.

Balshaw was born in West Yorkshire while his father played for Premiership club Leeds Tykes, before the family moved to Biarritz when Iain - an electrifying full-back/wing who scored three tries in England's iconic 2003 campaign - joined the cross-channel exodus to the French Top 14.

The Balshaws have remained in the luxurious Basque coastal city, known for its Belle Epoque architecture, Atlantic seafront casinos and world-class surfing.

"We came down in Biarritz in 2009 and we just loved the place," said Felix, who broke into the world's top 200 last month for the first time.

"I grew up in France and, as each day went by, I felt more and more French.

"Since I've been little, from when I started playing in Tennis Europe juniors, I have always had the French flag by my name."

Vickery's journey from World Cup winner to bodybuilder at 50

Balshaw pledging allegiance to his adopted country is understandable given the limited contact with his birthland.

Trips back across the English Channel have been "very rare" for the Balshaw children, largely restricted to Christmas family gatherings.

Their maternal grandmother lives in Bath, although Felix has never visited his father's hometown of Blackburn.

But the world number 178 is fully aware his dad will forever be ingrained in the fabric of English sporting history.

The then Bath player scored three tries in the pool stage of England's historic 2003 World Cup campaign, helping secure a 20-17 victory over Australia in the final when he came on as a second-half substitute.

On the eve of the biggest match of his career - facing fellow Frenchman Corentin Moutet in the Lyon Open second round - Felix tried to draw inspiration from watching highlights of his father playing in 2003.

"I just had a massive smile [watching] because I can say 'this is my dad'," he said.

"When he was at Biarritz I was always stood in a little corner in the stands with the rugby gang. It was very, very inspirational to watch him.

"As a father he's tough, but it's always important that he has a lot of experience in rugby, so he's got a lot of stuff to teach me.

"He's always been a great, great part of my life. He's always had my back."

Balshaw started playing tennis at the age of four, but unsurprisingly also had a talent for rugby.

At 13, he needed to make a choice about which sport he wanted to pursue more seriously with the prospect of a professional career looming.

"When I was little, and your father is a rugby champion, of course you always want to follow in his steps and do the same journey as him," Balshaw said.

"But I just felt that rugby was not going to be my sport.

"Tennis, I guess, is more difficult for me than rugby because it's an individual sport, but there was a little more fire in me [playing tennis].

"That meant it was the right choice to choose tennis."

Balshaw is essentially an inverted Arthur Fery - the French-born British number one who became a household name with a stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.

The pair actually met for the first time at this week's ATP 250 event in Lyon, where Balshaw beat Portuguese world number 56 Jaime Faria for his maiden win at tour level.

Possessing a Roger Federer-style one-handed backhand, and a Thor-inspired hammer celebration, Balshaw announced his arrival in some style.

Next week Balshaw will rise into the world's top 180, having starting the 2026 season ranked 718th.

His success will no doubt catch the attention of Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) chiefs, who are desperate to increase the pool of British players at the elite level.

Was Balshaw ever approached by the LTA to represent the country of his birth?

And was there ever a conversation with his parents about who he should represent?

"Maybe my parents are hiding stuff and I don't know, but I have never been personally contacted by the LTA," Felix said.

"I think for [my parents] the most important thing is if I'm happy, they'll be happy as well."

articles.title: El Chamartín acoge el Campeonato de España por equipos, una de las grandes citas de nuestro tenis
articles.standfirst: Del 26 al 28 de octubre el femenino y del 29 al 1 de noviembre el masculino
articles.summary: Del 26 al 28 de octubre el femenino y del 29 al 1 de noviembre el masculino
articles.body: Aunque el tenis es un deporte individual, el tenis por equipos ha sido consustancial al mismo desde sus comienzos -la Copa Davis data de 1903, para su homóloga femenina hubo que esperar hasta los años 60 pero tiene ya más de medio siglo y ya en los primeros tiempos eran populares los encuentros interclubes-. Modernamente a la BJK y la Copa Davis se han sumado la United Cup y la Laver Cup. Pero el principio es el mismo: unir a la épica individual la energía de luchar por un objetivo común. Y eso lo hace muy atractivo para los competidores. Como dijo Carlos Alcaraz tras la pasada Laver Cup, "doy instrucciones a quienes habitualmente son mis rivales en el circuito, aquí les doy instrucciones. Espero que me hagan caso. Me encanta jugar competiciones por equipos. Para mí es un honor participar. Me lo paso muy bien tanto dentro como fuera de la pista." Y la gran competición por equipos del tenis español está llamando a la puerta. Desde el próximo lunes 26 de octubre el C.T. Chamartín de Madrid será sede de los Campeonatos de España absolutos. Del 26 al 28 el femenino y del 28 al 31 el masculino. Tomarán parte muchos de los clubes más clásicos y reputados del tenis español, y no olvidemos que los clubes son la verdadera base del deporte: es allí donde los jóvenes jugadores dan sus primeros pasos, desde donde se inicia el camino a la élite y también el entorno al que quedan unidos muchos de los recuerdos más entrañables de los tenistas. De ahí la fidelidad de los mismos al club, y por tanto al torneo. Modernamente la colusión de los entornos profesional y amateur hace difícil que los líderes puedan tomar parte en este Campeonato de España por equipos, pero hasta bien entrados los años 90 no era raro ver en el mismo a quien poco antes -entonces se jugaba en noviembre-diciembre había estado disputando la Copa Davis o las Finales ATP y WTA. Este año estarán sobre las pistas del Chamartín, el club de origen de Rafael Jódar y Dani Mérida como últimos eslabones de una larga cadena, una buena representación de hombres y mujeres que rondan el 'top 200' ATP y WTA, lo que garantiza espectáculo de calidad, en la línea del amplio calendario de tenis profesional que se desarrolla normalmente en España y es una de las bases de su fortaleza tenística. El RCT Barcelona-1899 defenderá el título femenino conquistado el pasado año en Zaragoza. Las barcelonesas y las entonces subcampeonas, Valencia CT, son los principales favoritos en una edición que contará también con el CD Stadium Casablanca de Zaragoza, Real Murcia CT 1919, CT Chamartín, CA Montemar de Alicante, Real Zaragoza CT 1907 y CDE Tenis Madrid, equipo debutante tras el ascenso logrado el pasado año. En la competición masculina, el Real Murcia CT 1919 defenderá el título ganado en casa en la última edición. Junto a ellos estarán el CA Montemar, CT Valencia, CT Chamartín, Cercle Sabadellès 1856, Real Zaragoza CT y el Campus Tenis Club de Granada, que también jugará por primera vez en la elite. El RCT Tenis Barcelona es siempre equipo a batir como dominador histórico en ambas modalidades (32 de 52 títulos en categoría femenina y 35 de 55 en masculina), pero es el Real Murcia el defensor del título en categoría masculina mientras el RCT Barcelona lo es en femenina. A la presentación asistió 'Pepo' Clavet, entrenador de Alejandro Davidovich, junto a, entre otros, el presidente de la RFET, Miguel Díaz y el de la FTM, 'Tati' Rascón. Todos animaron a que nadie se pierda una cita cuya permanencia en el calendario es el mejor aval de su solidez y el compromiso con ella de clubes y tenistas. Además, la entrada es gratuita para el público.

articles.title: Rafael Jodar criticised for his ‘inexcusable’ behaviour at the Shanghai Masters
articles.summary: Rafael Jodar disappointed many with his behaviour at the Shanghai Masters. During his fourth-round win over Botic van de Zandschulp, Jodar was heard shouting...
articles.body:
Rafael Jodar disappointed many with his behaviour at the Shanghai Masters.

During his fourth-round win over Botic van de Zandschulp, Jodar was heard shouting at a ball boy , demanding he give him his towel. The Spaniard later apologised for the incident, but not before the 20-year-old received a wave of criticism.

Top tennis coach Brad Gilbert and former Grand Slam semi-finalist Andrea Petkovic have now discussed Jodar's behaviour during the latest episode of ' The Big T Podcast '.

Brad Gilbert says Rafael Jodar's behaviour towards 'vulnerable' ball kids is inexcusable

"Let's move on to Rafa Jodar and just speak about him for a little while, because he has now had a few run ins, I'm trying to be careful about this word, because during the French Open, there was a video where it seemed like he pushed a ball girl. I really have to say about this, that's why I didn't want to really bring it up, that video looked bad, but from a different angle, you could see that he didn't do anything to the ball girl, that's number one," said Petkovic .

"However, there have been a few situations, BG [Brad Gilbert], with Rafa Jodar , where our producer, Gary, wrote into our running order: Is Rafa Jodar the villain of the ATP Tour? What's your answer to that?"

"First of all, what an amazing first year the guy has had on tour. He's got a great chance to make the year-end championships. He's got a team of one, just his dad; he doesn't have anyone else. But the reason why Gary could say that about a villain, there are a lot of things that happen on a court, but one thing that is inexcusable, if you've ever been a ball kid and know that some of these kids are nervous doing it, you can never lose it on a ball kid," said Gilbert .

"Ok, you don't exactly know what the exact ramifications of what happened in Paris, the one where he literally snapped about not getting his towel and swearing at a ball kid, to me, is inexcusable.

"I understand players lose it; we've seen Medvedev lose it a lot, players snapping. That should be off-limits. He should literally watch that video, learn from it; if he gets mad, it should never have anything to do with the ball person again, because I feel like that's controllable. Losing and snapping at an umpire sometimes, or a decision on court, yourself, opponent… Not a ball person, who is very vulnerable."

Gilbert wasn't impressed by Jodar's behaviour whatsoever, although Petkovic was willing to show him more 'grace', given the Spaniard has only just turned 20 and is new to the tour.

"Most of the tournaments still work with kids, so it is a very bad look when you, I don't want to say attack, it's not like he physically attacked a kid, but when you snap at a kid, because they are children," she said.

"I don't want to defend it; the one thing I try to keep in mind is he's 19 years old. He's been thrown into the circus. One year ago, he didn't even have ball kids; he was playing little Challenger tournaments where he probably had to get his own balls. So I give him a little grace, but it can't continue to happen."

Jodar has been warned not to make the mistake again and has promised he won't. Whether he can keep that promise remains to be seen. Fans will keep a close eye on Jodar's behaviour over the coming months as he continues chasing an ATP Finals spot.

Rafael Jodar is in line to make his ATP Finals debut this year

The 20-year-old currently occupies the last ATP Finals qualification spot. He leads Alex de Minaur by 279 points and Novak Djokovic by 319 points. With 1,500 points up for grabs in Vienna/Basel and Paris, Jodar still has work to do before he can book his flights to Turin.

But even if he misses out on ATP Finals qualification, he can still be proud of a stellar breakthrough season. Looking to finish the year on a high, Jodar will return to action at the Swiss Indoors in Basel, which begins on Monday, October 26.

articles.title: Wrexham Open: Alicia Dudeney wins epic as British trio march on
articles.summary: Alicia Dudeney leads a great day for British players on day three of the Wrexham Open as she joins Jodie Burrage and Hannah Klugman in the quarter-finals.
articles.body:
Venue: Wrexham Tennis and Padel Centre Date: 18-25 October

Coverage: Watch live on BBC Sport online and BBC iPlayer

Alicia Dudeney led a great day for British players on day three of the Lexus Wrexham Open as she joined Jodie Burrage and Hannah Klugman in progressing to Friday's quarter-finals.

The in-form Dudeney extended her winning run to seven matches in the World Tennis Tour W100 event at Wrexham Tennis and Padel Centre, outlasting seventh seed Susan Bandecchi from Switzerland 6-3 6-7 (4-7) 6-4 in a match lasting two hours and 51 minutes.

She will now face French player Elsa Jacquemot in the last eight.

Dudeney was followed into the Carden Park Arena by Klugman, with the 17-year-old producing another excellent performance to beat higher ranked Czech player Anna Siskova 6-2 6-4.

Klugman, who reached the French Open junior girls' final last year and is currently ranked 341, will now play sixth seed Rebecca Sramkova from Slovakia.

Watch live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app.

Burrage ensured there would be three British players in action on Friday by beating fourth seed Noma Noha Akugue 6-1 7-6 (11-9).

She will next play Marina Bassols Ribera, the fifth seed, following the Spanish star's victory over Australian Lizette Cabrera.

There was a big upset elsewhere as top seed Anna Blinkova, the French player currently 72 in the world rankings, fell at the second-round stage as she lost 6-3 6-2 against Suzan Lamens from the Netherlands.

The form of the British trio has helped bolster home fans after reigning champion Mimi Xu, from Swansea, opted not to defend her title this year, instead competing at the W75 Saguenay tournament in Canada.

articles.title: ‘Every time I’m playing, it’s almost a win for me’: Yuki Bhambri on injuries and gratitude
articles.summary: ALMATY: Yuki Bhambri’s smile is revealing.
articles.body: ALMATY: Yuki Bhambri’s smile is revealing. It belongs to someone who has learnt to accept what life throws at him, not with resignation, but with the understanding that there is little point railing against what cannot be changed. You work with what you have, make the best of it and move on.The 34-year-old’s Zen-like equanimity has been forged in the storms he has weathered through much of his adult life. He began the 2026 season with good reason for optimism. Fresh off a first Grand Slam semifinal at the 2025 US Open, alongside close friend Michael Venus, Bhambri carried that momentum into the new year, climbing to a career-high No. 18 in the rankings in February.Then tennis did what life so often does, complicate plans. An elbow injury that required surgery kept Venus off the Tour, and when the New Zealander returned in March, the pair needed time to find their stride again. In August, at Winston-Salem, Bhambri injured his quad and he’s yet to regain full fitness.“That’s tennis for you,” Bhambri told TOI at the Almaty Arena. “That's why you have to respect players who are able to stay on Tour for so long. It's so difficult to do it year after year, to maintain a ranking, keep improving, keep playing and chasing those Grand Slams and Masters titles.”For Bhambri the injury has meant a step back, his ranking has slipped to No. 46.He’s playing the Almaty Open this week with American Ryan Seggerman, the duo are seeded four. Next he plays a Challenger in Seoul and will finish the season at the Paris Masters.“I've been in these situations before because of injuries, where you play for a year, a year and a half, and then have to stop,” he says. “But this time it's a little different. I've been able to play, but I haven't performed exactly as I would have liked. So it's been a learning curve, almost a fresh start to get back to competing for important events.”Starting over is a familiar exercise for Bhambri. Once Indian tennis's teenage prodigy, he won the Australian Open junior title at 16, became the junior world No. 1 and claimed a silver medal at the Youth Olympics. After he turned pro his singles journey was repeatedly interrupted by tendonitis in both knees.Some three years ago, he switched his focus to doubles.The Asian Games was a goal this year and Bhambri and Dhakshineswar Suresh were billed medal prospects. Bhambri’s movement was hampered by injury, and the pair bowed out in the quarterfinals.“It's disappointing how it panned out,” he says, a flicker of a smile on his face.Bhambri knows what an Asian Games medal feels like. At the 2014 Asian Games, he won two bronze medals, one in singles and the other in doubles.“I feel very fortunate that I did it a long time ago,” he says of the medals. “Hopefully, I'll get another chance four years down the line to improve on that.”There is a telling distinction in the way Bhambri talks about his career. He does not pretend that losing is easy, or that ambition has somehow evaporated with experience. He still wants to win, climb the rankings and compete at the biggest tournaments. But the years spent watching his career stall because his body was wounded may have altered his perspective.“Every time I'm playing, it's almost a win for me,” he says, his eyes following the players around him at the Almaty Arena. “Somewhere at the back of my mind, there's gratitude that I'm still here, still competing. You want to win everything, of course, but a small part of me considers just being here, competing at these events, a little win in itself.”Was there anger before the gratitude?“I've had different setbacks, but a lot of them have been about not being able to play,” he said. “Maybe it goes back to growing up in a country where a lot of these things weren't accessible. I was always handed down racquets from my sisters. You learnt quite early that if you broke one, you couldn't necessarily expect to get another. So breaking racquets or getting angry on court wasn't really an option, because you might not have anything to play with. Maybe some of that has stayed with me.”Perhaps that is where Bhambri's composure is tethered, not in some grand philosophy of sport or life, but in the practical understanding that what you have is worth looking after. The racquet had to last. The opportunity to play could not be taken for granted.Years later, the stakes are different, the racquets are his own and the ambitions considerably larger. Yet the instinct to work with what is in front of him remains.
